notes:
Now let me compile comprehensive verse-by-verse notes from all the material gathered.

# Proverbs 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1: "A wise son heeds his father's discipline, but a mocker does not listen to rebuke."

**Traditional Reading:** A wise child is the product and embodiment of a father's discipline — he listens, receives, and profits from parental instruction. The Hebrew is elliptical, literally "A wise son, his father's discipline," meaning he is the result of it. The line has a spiritual reach: the spiritually wise hear the instruction of Christ, the "everlasting Father" to His children, embracing and obeying the Gospel. By contrast, the "scorner" (mockers who scoff at sin and religion) refuses even rebuke — a stronger word than "instruction," showing he responds to no level of correction. Gill notes that such scorners, like Lot's sons-in-law or the sons of Eli and Samuel, scoff at the reproof itself. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/13.htm)

**Pulpit Commentary** emphasises the religious sphere: to be wise is to "hearken to the voice of Jehovah." All that God teaches — by inspired teachers, experience, inner revelation, and suffering — is "a father's instruction." The scorner has cast aside all reverential awe. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/13.htm)

**Matthew Henry:** "There is great hope of those that reverence their parents. There is little hope of any who will not hear those that deal faithfully with them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 2: "From the fruit of his lips a man enjoys good things, but the desire of the faithless is violence."

**Traditional Reading:** Wise, good speech brings tangible blessings — "eating good" by the fruit of one's mouth. The good man's words minister grace to hearers and also benefit himself. Gill notes that while a minister feeds others, he himself is nourished by words of faith and sound doctrine. The unfaithful (or "transgressors"), by contrast, "feed on violence" — both desiring it and having it returned upon their own heads. Poole says they shall have "that violence and injury returned upon themselves, which they have offered to others in word or deed." The Pulpit Commentary represents enjoyment under the figure of eating: the foundation of life-joy is one's inward state and social relations. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 3: "He who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin."

**Traditional Reading:** Restraint in speech preserves life; reckless talk courts ruin. Trapp compares guarding the mouth to a guard keeping the gates in a siege: "God hath set a double guard of lips and teeth before this gate, and yet, unless he himself set the watch, and keep the door, all will be lost." Clarke famously observes that God gave us two eyes and two ears but only one tongue (fenced with teeth) to indicate "though we hear and see much, we should speak but little." An old Arab proverb applies: "Take heed that your tongue does not cut your throat." The one who "opens wide his lips" — the rash, talkative, uncontrolled speaker — brings destruction. Gill notes this can apply naturally (trouble with authorities) and spiritually (blasphemy leading to perdition). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm)

**Matthew Henry:** "He that thinks before he speaks, that suppresses evil if he have thought it, keeps his soul from a great deal both of guilt and grief. Many a one is ruined by an ungoverned tongue." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 4: "The slacker craves yet has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied."

**Traditional Reading:** The lazy person does not lack desire — he craves plenty — but refuses the effort required to obtain it, so he has nothing. Bridges: "The sluggard craves the fruit of diligence without the diligence that gains it." Trapp: "Affection without endeavour is like Rachel — beautiful, but barren." Contrast this with the diligent, whose soul is "made fat" — fully satisfied with abundance. Clarke applies this spiritually: "We often hear many religious people expressing a desire to have more of the Divine life, and yet never get forward in it. How is this? The reason is, they desire, but do not stir themselves up to lay hold upon the Lord." Guzik notes that "soul" here primarily means "life," yet diligence in spiritual things brings spiritual riches. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html)

---

## v. 5: "The righteous hate falsehood, but the wicked bring shame and disgrace."

**Traditional Reading:** The righteous hate lying — not merely avoiding it but actually hating it, sharing God's own love of truth and hatred of the lie. The Hebrew speaks of a "word of falsehood." The wicked man, by contrast, is "loathsome" — the Hebrew word suggests causing a stench or spreading a foul smell. He makes himself repulsive and eventually comes to shame. Poole notes: "there being scarce any reproach which men more impatiently endure, and severely revenge, than that of being called or accounted a liar." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 6: "Righteousness guards the man of integrity, but wickedness undermines the sinner."

**Traditional Reading:** Righteousness — both God's imputed righteousness and the practical integrity of the blameless life — acts as a guard, preserving the upright in their way. It keeps them from fatal mistakes and crooked paths. But wickedness "overthrows" the sinner. The Hebrew literally calls him "sin" — the man of sin, given up to wicked courses, is overthrown by his own sin. Gill sees an allusion to the "man of sin" (2 Thessalonians 2:3), the antichrist figure, who shall be destroyed by his own wickedness. Matthew Henry: "An honest desire to do right, preserves a man from fatal mistakes, better than a thousand fine-drawn distinctions." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 7: "One pretends to be rich, but has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth."

**Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew uses a reflexive (hithpael) verb form, suggesting making oneself appear rich or poor — hence "pretends" or "feigns." Some parade as wealthy but possess nothing of real value; health, happiness, and peace cannot be bought. Morgan: "Our own age abounds with men who have made themselves rich, and yet have nothing." Conversely, some make themselves poor — through generosity or fixed spiritual priorities — yet possess great riches. Guzik sees Jesus Christ as the supreme example (2 Corinthians 8:9): "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich." Clarke notes two characters: "the rich poor man" and "the poor rich man." Matthew Henry adds a spiritual application: "There are many hypocrites, empty of grace, who will not be convinced of their poverty. There are many fearing Christians, who are spiritually rich, yet think themselves poor." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 8: "Riches may ransom a man's life, but a poor man hears no threat."

**Traditional Reading:** This verse points out that wealth has both advantages and disadvantages. Riches can ransom a life — as Benhadad's treasures saved him (1 Kings 20:34), or the men who bought off Ishmael (Jeremiah 41:8). Yet the rich man is a target for extortion, accusation, and ransom demands. The poor man, by contrast, "hears no rebuke" — meaning no threats or extortion can touch him, since he has nothing to give. As Morgan puts it: "if wealth has its advantages, so also has poverty. The rich man by his wealth may be able to conserve his life, but the poor man escapes the very dangers into which the rich are brought." Clarke observes: "In despotic countries, a rich man is often accused of some capital crime, and to save his life, though he may be quite innocent, is obliged to give up his riches; but the poor, in such countries, are put to no trouble." Bridges adds that spiritual redemption requires a far greater ransom: "What can a person give in exchange for his soul (Matthew 16:26)? It is too precious to be redeemed with corruptible silver and gold." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 9: "The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished."

**Traditional Reading:** The righteous are associated with light — a light that "rejoices" (the Hebrew suggests a joyful, bright shining). This light may be eclipsed or clouded temporarily, but it continues. The Septuagint reads "light is always for the righteous." The wicked have only a "lamp" (a smaller, artificial light), which will be "put out" in obscure darkness. Waltke notes the contrast of "the enduring wealth of the righteous with the extinction of the wicked and implicitly their wealth." Gill contrasts the sun (righteous) with the lamp (wicked) — lesser, less agreeable, and temporary. Clarke suggests "light" and "lamp" may also refer to posterity: the righteous have a joyous posterity; the wicked's line is cut off (citing 1 Kings 11:36; 15:4; Psalm 132:17). Matthew Henry: "the Spirit is their Light, he gives a fulness of joy: that of the wicked is as a lamp of their own kindling, easily put out." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 10: "Arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised."

**Traditional Reading:** Pride is the root cause of contention. The Hebrew has "only by pride" or "surely by pride" comes contention. Gill notes that an "empty man" (empty of knowledge) through pride will give contention. Clarke expands: "Perhaps there is not a quarrel among individuals in private life, nor a war among nations, that does not proceed from pride and ambition." He adds that "the salvation of Christ is a deliverance from pride, and a being clothed with humility. As far as we are humble, so far we are saved." By contrast, the "well-advised" — those humble enough to receive counsel — possess wisdom. Trapp gives a vivid image: "Pride is a dividing distemper; gouty swollen legs keep at a distance; bladders blown up with wind spurt one from another, and will not close; but prick them, and you may pack a thousand of them in a little room." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html)

---

## v. 11: "Dishonest wealth will dwindle, but what is earned through hard work will be multiplied."

**Traditional Reading:** Wealth obtained by "vanity" — dishonesty, fraud, speculation, gambling, or illicit means — has no staying power. It "will be diminished" or, as some render the Hebrew, comes "from a vapor" and evaporates. Clarke: "All fortunes acquired by speculation, lucky hits, and ministering to the pride or luxury of others, etc., soon become dissipated. They are not gotten in the way of Providence, and have not God's blessing, and therefore are not permanent." The alternative is "gathering by labour" — literally "by the hand," honest industry. The Targum interestingly renders it: "he that gathereth and giveth to the poor shall increase in substance." The Pulpit Commentary prefers the translation "Swindled wealth becomes small" and warns that hastily gotten wealth is generally hastily spent; "rapid fortune making, or sudden 'strokes of luck,' are certainly not to be envied in view of the good of the soul." Gill adds an eschatological application regarding Rome's ill-gotten riches: "that mass of riches which the church of Rome has got together by her vain and wicked practices… will in one hour come to nought (Revelation 18:17)." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 12: "Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life."

**Traditional Reading:** When hope's fulfillment is long delayed, the heart grows sick — dispirited, weak, ready to despair. Trapp: "How many see we lie languishing at hope's hospital, as he at the pool of Bethesda!" Yet when the desired thing finally comes, it is "a tree of life" — like the tree in Eden's garden, bringing comfort and vigour to both body and soul. Ross notes that "people can bear frustration only so long; they must have encouragement to continue," and suggests believers should help others realise their hopes whenever possible. Clarke elaborates: "Hope posts forward to realize the blessing. Delay in the gratification pains the mind; the increase of the delay prostrates and sickens the heart; and if delay sickens the heart, ultimate disappointment kills it." The Precept Austin material notes this is a psychological observation as much as a moral exhortation. Matthew Henry adds: "But spiritual blessings are chiefly intended." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_illustrations_2)

**Denominational note — General:** Most Protestant traditions read this as a general observation about the human condition under God's providence, applicable to both temporal and spiritual hopes. It is frequently cited in pastoral care and counselling contexts. Some traditions (Reformed, particularly) connect this to waiting on God's sovereign timing.

---

## v. 13: "He who despises instruction will pay the penalty, but the one who respects a command will be rewarded."

**Traditional Reading:** This proverb has strong religious significance. "The word" and "the commandment" most often refer to Scripture — Kidner calls this a "reminder that revealed religion is presupposed in Proverbs." The one who despises God's word "will be destroyed" (or, as Precept Austin explores from the Hebrew, "will be in debt to it" — owing a debt he cannot pay). This may be fulfilled through direct divine judgment or natural consequences. The one who "fears the commandment" — with reverential, filial awe, not slavish terror — will be rewarded. Clarke: "shall find it to be his highest interest, and shall be in peace or safety" (the Hebrew *shalam* carries the sense of wholeness, soundness, being uninjured). Spurgeon emphasises that this is a filial fear, not terror: "We have no terror of the Word, but we have a filial awe of it. We are not in fear of its penalties, because we have a fear of its commands." Precept Austin notes the Septuagint translates "rewarded" with *hugiaino* (hygiene) — being sound, healthy, whole — suggesting a present reward of soul-health, not only a future one. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-13-commentary ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html)

**Reformed perspective:** Bridges describes the fear of the commandment as "that affectionate reverence, by which the child of God bends himself humbly and carefully to his Father's law." Spurgeon: "Holy awe of God's Word is at a great discount. Men think themselves wiser than the Word of the Lord, and sit in judgment upon it." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-13-commentary)

---

## v. 14: "The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death."

**Traditional Reading:** The "law" or "teaching" of the wise — God's word mediated through wise instruction — is a fountain of life, a continual source of vitality and refreshment. It turns people from the "snares of death" — death pictured as a hunter laying traps. Waltke: "There is only one fountain of life, but there are many snares of death (cf. 2 Tim. 2:24-26)." Clarke suggests translating "The law is to the wise man a fountain of life" and sees an allusion to the garden of paradise, the tree of lives, the tempter, and the death that came through breaking God's law — the teaching of the wise reverses that curse. The Pulpit Commentary: "The teaching that is founded on Divine revelation is a source of life, and a safeguard against the snares of death." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 15: "Good understanding wins favor, but the way of the faithless is difficult."

**Traditional Reading:** A person of "good understanding" — prudence, insight, practical wisdom — gains favour with God and man. The way of the "transgressors" or faithless is "hard" — literally rugged, enduring, perpetual in its difficulty. Clarke gives the memorable remark: "Never was a truer saying; most sinners have more pain and difficulty to get their souls damned, than the righteous have, with all their cross-bearings, to get to the kingdom of heaven." Bridges: "They dream of a flowery path, but they make for themselves a hard way." Augustine said, "I was held before conversion, not with an iron chain, but with the obstinacy of my own will." Matthew Henry adds that "the service of sin is slavery; the road to hell is strewed with the thorns and thistles that followed the curse." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 16: "Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool displays his folly."

**Traditional Reading:** The prudent person not only possesses knowledge but acts upon it — wisdom is practical, not merely theoretical. The fool, by contrast, "lays open" or spreads out his folly for all to see, like a merchant displaying wares. Bridges: "Lacking this prudence, a fool exposes his folly. He pours out his wrath, vaunts his vanity, exposes his thoughtlessness, and exercises no judgment." Matthew Henry notes: "It is folly to talk of things of which we know nothing, and to undertake what we are no way fit for." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 17: "A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing."

**Traditional Reading:** A messenger bears serious responsibility. A wicked or unfaithful one "falls into mischief" — both causing harm and suffering consequences. A faithful ambassador (the word suggests an envoy) brings "health" — healing, soundness, wholeness. Waltke notes that in the ancient Near East, professional couriers enjoyed extraordinary status, were authorised to speak in the "I" style of their client, and had to be courageous and well-trained. Garrett notes the messenger "is an example of a person charged with a serious responsibility." Spiritually, this applies to ministers of the Gospel: unfaithful messengers do mischief and fall into it; faithful ones bring healing. The Septuagint intriguingly reads "a bold king" instead of "a wicked messenger," apparently reading *melek* (king) for *malak* (messenger). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html)

---

## v. 18: "Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored."

**Traditional Reading:** Refusing correction — disdaining it — leads to poverty and shame. Waltke lists the many causes of poverty in Proverbs (laziness, love of pleasure, talkativeness, wickedness, meanness) but says "this proverb points to a more fundamental problem, namely, the refusal… to listen to the instructions that correct these flaws." Yet "poverty due to moral failure brings disgrace, but poverty with virtue (Proverbs 17:1; 19:1), such as from injustice (Proverbs 13:23), is not disgraceful." Garrett: "Proverbs takes a balanced position; it neither dehumanizes the poor on the grounds that they are to blame for all their troubles nor absolves the individual of personal responsibility." The one who "regards a rebuke" — seriously considers it, receives it kindly, and reforms — will be honoured. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 19: "Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but turning from evil is detestable to fools."

**Traditional Reading:** Echoing v. 12, fulfilled desire is sweet — especially when achieved through hard work, discipline, and sacrifice. But the fool finds departing from evil to be an "abomination" — something loathsome. He is so in love with his sin that renouncing it is unthinkable. Morgan: "Men will not pay the price of departing from evil, and so fail of the sweetness of fulfilled desire." Bridges: "Holiness makes heaven; sin makes hell. So which place are the ungodly suited for? Hating holiness means that you are fit for hell." Waltke: "A person's life depends on finding his drives and appetites satisfied. The frustrated fool goes from failure to failure, but the gratified righteous go from strength to strength." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/)

---

## v. 20: "He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed."

**Traditional Reading:** Companionship shapes character. To "walk with" implies love, attachment, and regular association — and it is impossible not to imitate those we love. Clarke: "Show me his company, and I'll tell you the man." The companion of fools is assumed to be a fool himself and will share their destruction. Kidner quotes John Knox's translation of the Vulgate: "Fool he ends that fool befriends." Matthew Henry: "Multitudes are brought to ruin by bad company." This is one of the most practically applied proverbs in all traditions regarding choice of friends, marriage partners, and church fellowship. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 21: "Disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous."

**Traditional Reading:** Evil actively "pursues" sinners — it chases after them like a hunter. This is both by the natural consequences of sin and the active judgment of God. The righteous, by contrast, have "good" repaid to them — they reap what they have sown (Galatians 6:7-8). Matthew Henry: "When God pursues sinners he is sure to overtake them; and he will reward the righteous." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 22: "A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous."

**Traditional Reading:** A good man leaves an inheritance that spans generations — not only material wealth (honestly acquired, which tends to be permanent), but spiritual legacy: prayers, example, and advice remembered and quoted for generations. Clarke: "He files many a prayer in heaven in their behalf, and his good example and advices are remembered and quoted from generation to generation." The sinner's wealth, however, is "laid up for the just" — God in His providence transfers it, as in the case of the Egyptians' wealth given to Israel at the Exodus. Matthew Henry: "The servant of God who is not anxious about riches, takes the best method of providing for his children." Clarke quotes the Latin proverb: *De male quaesitis non gaudet tertius haeres* — "The third generation shall not possess the goods that have been unjustly acquired." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

**Denominational note — Prosperity/Word of Faith:** Though not documented in the specific sites searched, this verse is commonly cited in prosperity teaching to support the idea that God guarantees believers material wealth and a multi-generational inheritance. The traditional reading, however, emphasises spiritual legacy and honestly acquired goods under God's providence, not a mechanistic promise of wealth.

---

## v. 23: "Abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away."

**Traditional Reading:** Even the "fallow ground" (untilled land) of the poor contains potential for abundant food — the poor could thrive through industry. But injustice ("want of judgment") sweeps it away. Clarke interprets this as the poor's own mismanagement: "O, how much of the poverty of the poor arises from their own want of management! They have little or no economy, and no foresight." However, the verse may also point to systemic injustice — the poor are cheated of what could sustain them. Both readings are found in the tradition. Matthew Henry: "The poor, yet industrious, thrive, though in a homely manner, while those who have great riches are often brought to poverty for want of judgment." (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

---

## v. 24: "He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently."

**Traditional Reading:** This is one of the most discussed proverbs on child discipline. All major commentators agree the verse commends loving, timely correction. The Hebrew *shevet* ("rod") represents parental authority and the means of punishment. "Betimes" (Hebrew *shachar*, "early in the morning") means either in the morning of life (before habits harden) or promptly after the offence. The Pulpit Commentary: "A father who truly wishes well to his son keeps him betimes under strict discipline… he who is indulgent toward his child when he ought to be strict, acts as if he really wished his ruin." Gill: "Such fond love is no better than hatred; and, if he really hated him, he could scarcely do a more ill thing by him than not to correct him for a fault." Matthew Henry: "He acts as if he hated his child, who, by false indulgence, permits sinful habits to gather strength, which will bring sorrow here, and misery hereafter." Clarke, quoting Holden: "By the neglect of early correction the desires (passions) obtain ascendancy; the temper becomes irascible, peevish, querulous. Pride is nourished, humility destroyed." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm ; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/13-24.htm)

**Reformed (A.W. Pink / Monergism):** Pink strongly emphasises the use of the rod and parental authority: "The teaching of Scripture is crystal clear on this point. 'Foolishness is bound in the heart of the child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him'… Spare the rod, and you spoil the child. If you don't use the rod on him — you lay up one for your own back." However, Pink balances this: "It should hardly need pointing out that the above Scriptures are far from inculcating that a reign of terror is to mark the home life. Children can be governed and punished in such a way so that they do not lose their respect and affections toward their parents." He warns against punishing "to vent your own rage." (Monergism: https://www.monergism.com/word-parents)

**Methodist/Wesleyan (John Wesley):** Wesley is emphatic: "If you do fear God, how dare you suffer a child above a year old to say, 'I will do' what you forbid, or, 'I won't do' what you bid, and to go unpunished? … Do not 'spare the rod, and spoil the child.' If you have not the heart of a tiger, do not give up your child to his own will, that is, to the devil. Though it be pain to yourself, yet pluck your offspring out of the lion's teeth. Make them submit, that they may not perish. Break their will, that you may save their soul." Wesley's focus is on conquering the child's will early. (CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/sermons.vi.xliii.html)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill connects the failure to discipline with the sin of Eli: "which was the sin of good old Eli, and both he and his sons suffered for it." He emphasises "chasteneth him betimes" as "every morning" or as soon as the fault is committed. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/13.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Guzik says simply: "Proper discipline for a child comes from both wisdom and love. Such correction will be done promptly, reinforcing the connection between the correction and error of the child." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-13/)

**General note on denominational differences:** Historically, all the major Protestant traditions represented here affirm corporal discipline in principle, though with varying emphasis. The key differences are not between traditions (all agree the rod is necessary) but between historic Christian teaching and modern secular parenting philosophies that reject physical discipline. All the traditional commentators warn against abuse or angry punishment while affirming loving, measured correction. The phrase "spare the rod, spoil the child" (not a direct biblical quote but a proverb derived from this and related verses) remains controversial in modern Christian parenting debates, but the traditional commentaries are unanimous in affirming the principle.

## v. 25: "A righteous man eats to his heart's content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty."

**Traditional Reading:** The righteous person eats "to the satisfying of his soul" — his desires are moderate, his appetite is content with what God provides, and he is satisfied. The wicked, by contrast, though using every expedient to acquire more — even rapine and wrong — is frequently in real want, and always dissatisfied. Matthew Henry: "It is the misery of the wicked, that even their sensual appetites are always craving. The righteous feeds on the word and ordinances, to the satisfying of his soul with the promises of the gospel, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Bread of life." Clarke: "A contented mind is a continual feast. At such feasts he eats not." This verse concludes the chapter by returning to the theme of satisfaction — the righteous are satisfied, the wicked are not — tying together the chapter's emphasis on the outcomes of wisdom versus folly. (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-13.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/13.htm)

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

1. **v. 24 (the rod):** All surveyed traditions (Reformed/Baptist/Methodist/Pentecostal) affirm the principle of loving corporal discipline. Differences are of tone: Wesley stresses breaking the child's will; Pink balances authority with gentleness; Guzik emphasises promptness and love. None endorse abusive or angry punishment.

2. **v. 12 (hope deferred):** All traditions read this as a general observation about human psychology under God's providence. Reformed teachers (via Spurgeon/Bridges) especially connect it to waiting on God's sovereign timing and the "already/not yet" of Christian hope.

3. **v. 22 (inheritance):** The traditional consensus is that the "inheritance" includes spiritual legacy, not merely material wealth. This stands in tension with prosperity/Word of Faith readings that treat it as a guarantee of material wealth transfer to believers.

4. **v. 13 (despising the word):** Reformed and Baptist teachers (Spurgeon, Bridges, Gill) particularly emphasise the authority and infallibility of Scripture in their treatment of this verse, while the Methodist Clarke emphasises the practical consequences of obedience.

*Modern scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey) and Catholic/Orthodox readings could not be obtained within search limits for this chapter.*
